sentences.text: The openings in the skull are shaped like ellipses, differing from the nearly round holes seen in related species like Stolokrosuchus.
Unlike modern crocodiles where the optic cavity is sealed at the back, the optic recess in this animal opens downward.
The bone at the back of the skull forms a clear U-shape because the bone above it pushes it downward.
Two large bones called otoccipitals cover the back of the braincase, creating a wide U-shaped joint with the supraoccipital bone.
The laterosphenoid bone builds the front side wall of the braincase and is made of two layers separated by a ridge.
A subrectangular plate at the front of the braincase widens toward the top and connects to other internal structures.
Specific ridges on the cheekbones match features found in other members of the Peirosauria group.
Teeth linked to this animal are cone-shaped with weak roots and moderate side-to-side flattening.
These teeth have small bumps on their cutting edges and enamel with long wavy lines, similar to those of Hamadasuchus.
The cast of the brain inside the skull looks like that of modern gharials and freshwater crocodiles, with broad front sections tapering to a spade shape.
Spines around the brain and side ridges are rare features known only in a few other ancient crocodilian relatives.
The main specimen, cataloged as RRBP 08630, was gathered in 2008 at a site named Namba 2.
All fossils of this genus were discovered about 25 kilometers south of Lake Rukwa in southwestern Tanzania.
Scientists Joseph J. W. Sertich and Patrick M. O'Connor gave the animal its name in 2014.
Although the primary specimen has no teeth, some teeth from the same rock layer have been tentatively assigned to it.
Computer scans revealed most of the internal brain shape, though some details are hidden by damage or rock material.
Certain brain features suggest this creature might have lived more on land than some water-loving relatives.
Researchers describe the animal as having a medium-to-large body size.
The pituitary gland area is noted as being quite small, with the hollow facing almost downward.
Evolutionary studies usually place Rukwasuchus within the group Peirosauria.
Its family placement is debated, with some placing it in Peirosauridae and others in Itasuchidae.
This genus is monotypic, meaning it contains only one species, Rukwasuchus yajabalijekundu.
Analyses suggest this lineage split after Kinesuchus and Stolokrosuchus but before most South American forms.
Recent work by Ruiz and Wilberg places it in either the subfamily Pepesuchinae or the family Itasuchidae.
The broader family group for this animal is Peirosauridae.
It belongs to the class Reptilia.
The species Rukwasuchus yajabalijekundu serves as the type species for the genus.
Fossils are found only in the Namba Member of the Galula Formation in Tanzania.
This environment was wetter and sub-humid with soil matching an open forest, following a shift from the drier Mtuka Member below.
The animal lived between 100.5 and 72.2 million years ago during the Cenomanian to Campanian stages.
